client: I lost my job last month, and I can't stop worrying about how we're going to pay the bills. My wife keeps telling me it'll be okay, but I feel like a failure for not being able to provide right now. I'm not sure talking about it will help when what I really need is another job.
therapist: I hear how deeply this job loss is affecting you, both practically and emotionally—it makes complete sense you'd feel this worry and self-doubt during such a difficult transition. When you say you feel like a failure, what specific thoughts come up about what this situation means about you?

client: I keep thinking that if I were smarter or more capable, I wouldn’t have lost my job in the first place. It feels like this proves I’m not good enough, and I worry I’ll never find something as stable again. It’s hard not to feel like I let myself and everyone around me down.
therapist: It sounds like your mind is connecting the job loss directly to your worth as a person, which must feel incredibly heavy to carry. I wonder if we could gently examine whether there might be other factors—like company changes or economic shifts—that also played a role here? What might you say to a close friend who was in this same situation?

client:
I get what you're saying about other factors, but it's hard not to take it personally when I was the only one on my team let go. I'd probably tell a friend it wasn't their fault, but with myself, it just feels different - like maybe if I'd worked harder or been more valuable, they would have kept me. 

The economic shift explanation doesn't really help because I keep replaying all the little mistakes I made in my head, wondering if those were the reasons.
therapist: It's understandable that this feels so personal when you were the only one let go—that distinction would make anyone question their value. When you replay those small mistakes, do you think it's possible you're focusing on them while overlooking all the contributions you made during your time there?

client:
I know logically that I did contribute, but it's hard to focus on that when the mistakes feel so glaring. Every time I try to think about the good work I did, my mind just jumps back to that one time I missed a deadline or when I stumbled during a presentation. It's like my brain won't let me remember anything positive. 

And honestly, even if I did make contributions, they clearly weren't valuable enough since I'm the one who got cut. That's what keeps eating at me - if my work had really mattered, they would have kept me, right?
therapist: It sounds like your mind is filtering out the positive aspects of your work and amplifying the perceived negatives, which can make it feel like those contributions weren't meaningful—even though they likely were. I wonder if we could explore the idea that being let go might not solely reflect your value, but could also be influenced by factors like budgets, restructuring, or shifting priorities. How might it feel to hold space for both your strengths and the reality that layoffs often aren't personal?

client:
I get what you're saying about layoffs not always being personal, but it's hard not to take it that way when I was the only one on my team let go. I keep replaying all the times my manager gave me feedback, wondering if those were warning signs I missed. 

The idea of focusing on my strengths feels impossible right now because all I can see are the mistakes I must have made. If I was really valuable, wouldn't they have found a way to keep me?
therapist: I hear how painful this is—being the only one let go naturally makes the situation feel intensely personal, and it's understandable you're searching for explanations in past feedback. When you think about those feedback moments, do you recall any that were actually positive, or is your mind only showing you the critical ones right now?

client: I guess there were a few positive comments here and there, but they feel meaningless now. All I can focus on is that one time my manager said I needed to be more proactive in meetings. It's like my brain keeps replaying that moment on loop, trying to figure out if that's why they chose me for layoffs.
therapist: It makes sense that the critical feedback stands out so vividly—our brains tend to fixate on perceived threats, especially during times of stress like this. I wonder if we could try an experiment: what would it feel like to hold both that feedback and the positive comments in your mind at the same time, like weighing two objects in your hands?

client: I get what you're saying about holding both the negative and positive feedback in my mind, but it feels almost impossible. The criticism just feels so much heavier, like it overshadows everything else. Even when I try to think about the positive comments, they don’t feel as real or meaningful—like they don’t matter as much. It’s like my brain dismisses them instantly.
therapist: It sounds like your mind is automatically discounting the positive feedback, which must make it feel impossible to see a balanced picture of your work. What do you think might happen if we explored why those positive comments feel less "real" to you than the critical ones?

client: I don't know, it's like the positive comments just bounce off me while the negative ones stick. Even when people say nice things about my work, part of me thinks they're just being polite or don't really mean it. Maybe it's because the critical feedback confirms what I already believe about myself.
therapist: That makes so much sense—when we already believe we're not good enough, our minds naturally cling to evidence that supports that belief while dismissing anything that contradicts it. How might it feel to consider that both the positive and negative feedback could be equally true, even if they don't feel that way right now?

client: I get what you're saying logically, but it's hard to really believe the positive stuff could be true when the negative thoughts feel so much more real. When someone gives me a compliment, my brain immediately finds reasons why they're just being nice or don't really mean it. It's exhausting.
therapist: It sounds like your mind has developed this automatic reflex to protect you from potential disappointment by dismissing positive feedback—and I can hear how exhausting that constant mental filtering must be. What would it feel like to notice when that reflex happens, and just observe it with curiosity rather than immediately believing it?

client: I get what you're saying about observing the reflex, but it's like my brain just automatically rejects any compliment before I even have a chance to notice it happening. When someone says something nice, I immediately feel this wave of discomfort and start listing reasons why they're wrong. It's not even a conscious choice.
therapist:
I hear how deeply ingrained this pattern is—it's not just thoughts you're having, but an almost physical reaction of discomfort that happens before you can even catch it. That automatic rejection must feel both exhausting and frustrating to experience. 

What do you think might happen if, just for a moment, we imagined that someone's compliment could be as valid as your self-criticism? Not necessarily true or false—just that both perspectives might have equal weight?
